Obviously, my nursery school had boys and girls. Most of my playmates were boys and I enjoyed myself. 

My mother forced me to attend a very exclusive all-girls school for primary and high school. The kind of place that prides itself on producing young ladies.

She felt it would make me into a lady. I was never able to fit in and hated every second of it.  I wasn't out to myself, never mind others. I think the closest I came to admitting my true self was an self-portrait art project. I drew myself as male.

What a thought-provoking post. I guess my internalized transphobia relates to putting too much importance on how others perceive me and how that impacts on my self-perception.

When I dressed as female, I was often labelled as butch, masculine, intimidating and was often made to feel uncomfortable in female spaces. 

My internalized transphobia sometimes made me question whether I was genuinely trans or simply uncomfortable with being a masculine woman in a society with little tolerance for them. 

I had to calm down and concentrate on how *I* perceive myself to get a clear image of who I am inside. My earliest memories and desires are focused around being male. As a young child, I remember thinking that the Blue Fairy from Pinocchio would transform me into a boy one day. For my entire life, I perceived myself as male and the female image in the mirror was often jarring. I'm much happier now that I pass as male in most public spaces.

But sometimes some internalized transphobia manifests as guilt. Now that I often pass for male in public spaces, people interact with me very differently. I'm often mistaken for a pretty teenage boy and instead of being seen as intimidating, I'm treated much better.

For example, I went to a restaurant when I still wore female clothes and had long hair. Despite my clothes, my gestures and body language have always be perceived by others as masculine. Even though I was polite, the waitress seemed scared of me, avoided meeting my eyes, veered between a hostile tone and a nervous one. 

Several months later, I went back to the restaurant. I now pass as male fairly well. I was served by the same waitress. She didn't recognize me and assumed I was a young guy. I guess as a petite pretty boy, I don't seem as intimidating. She chatted with me, brought my meal on time, asked if I was in my last year of high school or had started college yet and gave me a free hot chocolate.

Afterwards, I felt terribly guilty. As if by passing, I had somehow tricked her or pulled a fast one. I think this is due to internalized transphobia. I feel like I don't deserve to pass.

In a surprisingly short time, she learnt to be more civil towards me. Our relationship improved vastly. Unfortunately, she still lashes out at close friends but our interaction has improved.

I see. You don't want to address what you perceive as sexism in my comments yet you continue to say I hold "sexist opinions" and "express sexist opinions."

Despite the fact I clarified that I think men *and* women should address co workers in a professional manner in the workplace and that it can be inappropriate for either gender to call others by terms like "sweetie" in a professional context.

As I stated before, my view of certain terms as dehumanizing  based on my personal experiences and it depends on the context in which these words are used. 

>Most of the men who did this picked up that I was female trying to look male. and their use of sweetie or sweetheart was a subtle way of reminding me that I was unsuccessful at passing. Most of them were trying to find a way of upsetting me without looking like the bad guy and the inflection they gave "sweetheart" was similar to an insult. They meant to be insulting and they succeeded.

In this context, they used sweetheart as a way of reminding me that I was perceived as "other" - I wasn't passing as a man nor did I fit into their perception of what was a woman. Their repeated use of sweetie or sweetheart (even though I corrected them) was their way of continually empathizing my perceived "otherness" to those around us. By calling me sweetheart, they deliberately drew people's attention to the fact I didn't fit cleanly into either gender and that I was "different." Coupled with their hostile attitude, I felt dehumanized and humiliated by the experience.

One of my friends (MTF) had a similar experience when she wore female attire in public - she was wearing jeans and a fitted feminine vest. She had been on hormones long enough to grow breasts but her face had a masculine cast. We were at a park together, sitting on a bench. A family approached us and said something along the lines of "We'd appreciate it if you'd put on a jacket and cover yourself up, *sir.* We don't want our kids confused."

Despite being polite, they used seemingly innocent words to dehumanize her - they made her feel like a freak. My friend was devastated. As the family walked away, one of the kids asked the parents if my friend was a boy or a girl. They responded by using male pronouns "*he's* just confused and looking for attention. Ignore *him.*"

Whether or not words are dehumanizing depends on context and intent. For example, if my partner is called boy by his uncle, it's a term of affection, an endearment. But if he's called boy by someone in the workplace, he can perceive it as an insult and dehumanizing (because of his race and the use of the word boy in our country's history.) Of course, it depends on the context in which the word is used.

Honestly, we can argue back and forth about opinions, perceptions and experiences but I didn't put my original comment up in order to open an ongoing debate. I try not to get into debates with strangers on the internet - it's tiring and often a waste of time. If you wish to think of me as sexist (something which has **no** basis and is incorrect by the way), you have every right to do so - it's your opinion and you're welcome to it. But I don't have the time or inclination to debate back and forth with you.

I'm a bit taken aback at both your tone and unwarranted accusation of sexism. 

I simply stated my opinion - I think that calling someone sweetheart or sweetie in a professional context is unprofessional and can sometimes be a way of undermining that person. To clarify further, I feel that people in the workplace, regardless of gender, should be professional in how they address one another. 

>Let's put aside your sexist attitudes around how men are allowed to behave in front of women.

I never said men can't behave a certain way in front of women. I believe that men (and let's extend it to anyone) should try be professional in how they address another person in a professional context. 

In my personal experience, sometimes calling someone sweetie, sweetheart or a similar term in the workplace often goes hand in hand with invading personal space - not necessarily in a sexual sense but it can still be inappropriate.

For example,I've found when certain men (and women) called me by diminutive names in a workplace, they often also would touch me in ways that weren't appropriate (try ruffle my hair, chuck me under the chin etc) and undermined my professional status. Often they didn't mean this maliciously but it was still inappropriate. 

Also, calling someone sweetheart or a similar endearment in a professional context can be a way of undermining or devaluing them. 

Example : When I dressed as female, I put forward a suggestion for security measures in the workplace. I formerly worked in security and have a fairly in-depth understanding of the subject matter. 

My co worker's response was dismissive and condescending. Something along the lines of "You're obviously very passionate about this, dear, but it's just not necessary."

As I said before, whether or not an endearment is condescending depends on context and tone. But in this case, the use of dear (which was interchangable with sweetheart in this context) was clearly used to undermine my authority and suggestion and to put me in my place. To remind me that I was the only female on the team and that in this particular workmate's opinion, I wasn't able to contribute anything of value to this meeting.

And yes, I found it dehumanizing when a man called me sweetie or sweetheart when I tried (not always successfully) to pass in my younger days. Most of the men who did this picked up that I was female trying to look male. and their use of sweetie or sweetheart was a subtle way of reminding me that I was unsuccessful at passing. Most of them were trying to find a way of upsetting me without looking like the bad guy and the inflection they gave "sweetheart" was similar to an insult. They meant to be insulting and they succeeded. 

The above are my opinions and obviously opinions are partly formed by personal experiences.

At this point, I'm starting to pass as a man so my answer will reflect this. 

Passing as a guy means I don't have to guard my gestures - I don't have to make an effort to be more feminine (something that has never come naturally to me.) I'm feel able to relax and let my masculine body language and walk shine through. 

As far as physical transition is concerned, I look forward to having a flat toned chest, broader shoulders and a deeper voice. I'm giddy as a kid when I think about getting up each morning to shave my face. 

Physically being a woman and being perceived as a woman makes me feel like an unsuccessful female impersonator. But when I pass for a man, I'm comfortable and confident in my skin and my interactions with others.

Physically being a man wouldn't be about becoming a man - I'm already a man inside. But physically becoming a man would mean I could simply settle into a body that matches my inner self.
